---
title: "2. The Argument"
---

Chapter 1 introduced the three Conditions any genuine change requires: Temporality, Spatiality, and Physicality, each paired with its bearer in Reality (Time, Space, and Substance). The question now is stronger: are they merely features of this world, or conditions any possible reality must meet?

The proof turns on a single fact no one can consistently deny — that change is possible. From that fact, it argues that the three structural Conditions are not local features our universe happens to possess, but conditions any reality must meet.

What makes this more than the assertion of that claim is the standard the chapter holds itself to. Each premise states its exact burden, distinguishes role-level from type-level content, and identifies the rival commitment a critic may reject. Some alternatives collapse; others remain coherent rival semantics and are carried forward rather than mislabeled as contradictions. The proof is built to be climbed one step at a time, beginning with the global modal domain it runs in ([§2.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-1)).

By *Nature*, the chapter means the single structure these three Conditions jointly constitute — not three requirements that happen to coincide, and not a necessary being standing alongside contingent things. That this structure holds of necessity is not assumed here but earned step by step, and the stages are gathered into the finished line only at the close ([§2.8](the-argument.html#sec-2-8)).

## 2.1 The S5 Pipeline {#sec-2-1}

The question is whether a possibility, once secured, is itself necessary: if something is really possible, does that possibility hold in every world? Establishing that modal rule is this section's whole work. Showing that the possibility of change in particular is necessary comes later, with the Cartesian witness of [§2.2](the-argument.html#sec-2-2) — and the order matters, since the rule has to be earned before there is any possibility to lift with it.

The answer turns on the scope of *real possibility*, fixed in [§1.2.1](groundwork.html#sec-1-2-1) as a determination Reality settles rather than as what is reachable from one local world-state. Let W be the complete range of worlds Reality permits: a proposition is possible when it is true at some member of W and necessary when true at every member. Everything that follows rests on a single commitment, that every point of evaluation ranges over the same W. That commitment is earned at the Bottleneck ([§2.1.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-5)), not assumed here, and what it yields is S5's characteristic principle without importing the later claim that T, S, and Φ hold in every world.

The pipeline runs four stages before the objection arrives. Modal Bivalence ([§2.1.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-1)) supplies the classical two-verdict grammar: ◇P or ¬◇P. The Bilateral Frame ([§2.1.2](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-2)) requires the argument to track both verdicts. Modal Constitution ([§2.1.3](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-3)) distinguishes occupancy from invariance and establishes, from a logical truth ⊤ on one side and a contradiction ⊥ on the other, that both poles are necessarily occupied: the frame is never empty, though nothing substantive is yet claimed to fill it. Modal Stability ([§2.1.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-4)) then gives the fixed-domain derivation of T, S4, B, the Euclidean principle, and its bilateral companion.

The remaining objection is precise: perhaps each world owns a different possibility horizon. The Bottleneck ([§2.1.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-5)) answers by separating local reachability from global real possibility. A local accessibility relation may vary; the complete domain of Reality's possibilities does not become a different domain merely because evaluation moves to another member. The Parasitic Negation Lemma, stated there, rules out a domain's onset from its own external absence, and the Transition Closure ([§2.1.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-6)) applies that result to C-status under structural accessibility; both reinforce the account of structural incapacity without carrying the fixed-domain derivation of proposition-wise S5. What the Bottleneck defends is the global operator, not the Necessity of Nature in advance.

::: {.argument}
**Necessary Possibility** · *The Global-Domain Line*

1. W is the complete range of worlds Reality permits.

1. ◇P means that P is true at some world in W.

1. □P means that P is true at every world in W.

1. If ◇P, a world u in W witnesses P.

1. Every world evaluates real possibility over the same W, so u remains a witness everywhere.

1. Therefore whatever is possible is necessarily possible: ◇P → □◇P.

1. If no world in W witnesses P, that absence likewise holds throughout W: ¬◇P → □¬◇P.

:::

The result is schematic. It fixes the modal status of any proposition once that status is known, but establishes no substantive antecedent. The Cartesian witness in [§2.2](the-argument.html#sec-2-2) supplies the one possibility the canonical proof needs.

Two Readings ([§2.1.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-7)) separates the diachronic and cross-world indices of the one theorem; the grounding and transfer questions surrounding it are tested at §[§2.1.8](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-8)–2.1.9; and Necessary Possibility ([§2.1.10](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-10)) assembles the result.

*What is established.* Real possibility is global over one domain W; local reachability is a distinct relative modality. On that fixed-domain reading, S5 and the bilateral invariance of modal status follow without assuming the Triconditions. The proof can therefore use Necessary Possibility to derive their necessity later without circling back through its own conclusion.

### 2.1.1 Modal Bivalence {#sec-2-1-1}

Modal Bivalence is the exhaustiveness of the book's two primitive modal verdicts. For any contentful claim P, either P is really possible (◇P) or it is not (¬◇P). Since impossibility is defined as the negation of possibility, the formal disjunction ◇P ∨ ¬◇P is classical excluded middle applied to a modal predicate. It records the grammar of the framework; it does not by itself establish any substantive fact about which propositions are possible.

::: {.premise}
**Modal Bivalence** · **P1** · *Premise 1*

For any contentful claim, either it is really possible or it is not: the two modal verdicts are exhaustive. ∀P: ◇P ∨ ¬◇P.


:::

The grammar fixes modal status, not truth, and the two come apart. A claim can be unsettled in truth — the next coin flip will land heads — while being settled in modal status: heads and tails are both possible before either becomes actual. Vagueness raises a different problem. A string that fails to determine a proposition does not yet supply a third modal status; it fails to provide a content to which either verdict can apply.

A genuine challenge to the two-verdict framework must therefore specify what it rejects: truth-aptness, classical negation, exhaustiveness, exclusivity, or the consequence rules used downstream. These are live options, not verbal confusions. A dialetheist such as Graham Priest challenges truth-value exclusivity: some propositions may be both true and false. That alone does not yield ◇P ∧ ¬◇P, because ¬◇P states that P is impossible, not merely that P is false. To challenge modal exclusivity here, the dialetheist must extend the glut to the modal predicate itself, allowing both ◇P and its negation. The disjunction ◇P ∨ ¬◇P can remain true on that proposal while the classical claim that exactly one disjunct holds fails. Paraconsistent and intuitionist positions may instead revise what follows from a contradiction or which reductios are licensed.

This section adopts both exhaustiveness and exclusivity as part of its classical framework without pretending that the first alone supplies the second. The later replies are correspondingly limited: [§2.7.2](the-argument.html#sec-2-7-2) asks whether logical revision can furnish a model of the Null State without the defending practice instantiating the Conditions, and [§5.3.4](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-4) runs the catuṣkoṭi corner by corner while preserving the wider dispute over positive metaphysical thesis-making.

The work of Modal Bivalence is limited but necessary. It fixes the two verdicts over which the later invariance theorem ranges. It does not prove that modal status is world-invariant, that both poles are occupied, or that any particular proposition is possible. Those are separate results.

*What is established.* Every contentful proposition receives one of the two modal verdicts under the classical framework used here: ◇P or ¬◇P. The result is modal exhaustiveness, not yet modal invariance.[^2-1-1-bivalence-ch4]

[^2-1-1-bivalence-ch4]: Fictionalism questions whether modal statements bear truth values at all ([§4.4.4](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-4)); dialetheist and paraconsistent revisions of classical exclusivity or consequence are met in operation, where [§2.7.2](the-argument.html#sec-2-7-2) tests the logical-revisionist rescue of the Null State and [§5.3.4](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-4) runs the catuṣkoṭi, the four-cornered tetralemma, against the necessity of the Conditions; dappled-world and deflationist views question whether one global modal domain is available ([§4.1.8](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-8)); and quietism doubts that the disjunction is meaningful ([§4.1.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-9)).

### 2.1.2 Bilateral Frame {#sec-2-1-2}

Modal Bivalence is bilateral; the rest of the proof works on both modal statuses. This subsection fixes that bilateral reading explicitly, because it diverges from how many modal arguments are usually run.

A one-sided reading of Modal Bivalence would emphasize only possibility: there are possibilities, and the question is what underwrites them. The Necessity-of-Nature proof refuses that asymmetry. Possibility and impossibility matter equally. The argument needs witnesses under both statuses because the *modal constraint* is identified by its bilateral work: what permits some change and prohibits other change. A constraint that only permits is not yet the modal constraint on change; it is a permission. A constraint that only prohibits is not yet the modal constraint on change; it is a prohibition. Whatever it is about Reality that fixes the modal status of change has to do both, and the proof has to engage both.

This bilateral framing is implicit in Modal Bivalence itself (the modal constraint does permission-work and prohibition-work alike), but it is now made structurally explicit. The requirement then propagates through the chapter. Cartesian Certainty ([§2.2](the-argument.html#sec-2-2)) supplies bilateral witnesses: some change is possible, some change is not. The account of what fixes modal status quantifies over the constraint itself, abstracting from which status it fixes. The Structural Requirement identifies the modal constraint with the three Conditions, which are bilateral in the same way: Temporality permits succession and prohibits reversal; Spatiality permits coexistence and prohibits double occupancy; Physicality permits qualitative change and prohibits causal disconnection.

*What is established.* The result is a chapter that engages every premise in both modal-status directions. There is no shortcut through possibility alone.[^2-1-2-bilateral-frame-ch4]

[^2-1-2-bilateral-frame-ch4]: The bilateral reading of Modal Bivalence (the requirement that the modal constraint do permission-work and prohibition-work alike) meets its objections in Chapter 4. The canonical one-sided position is the Humean denial of necessary connection, which grants permissions but resists prohibitions as anything beyond regularity ([§4.1.4](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-4)). Lewis presses whether plenitude permits everything and so loses the prohibition side ([§4.4.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-1)), and fictionalism presses one-sided modal commitment ([§4.4.4](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-4)). Williamson's necessitism is the closest ally on bilateral modal invariance ([§4.4.6](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-6)), and dappled-world accounts ask whether the bilateral reading scales beyond local domains ([§4.1.8](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-8)).

### 2.1.3 Modal Constitution {#sec-2-1-3}

Modal status answers to Reality's constitution rather than to how any particular world is arranged.[^2-1-3-invariance-scope] If that constitution is invariant, what is possible cannot lapse into impossibility and what is impossible cannot become possible: ◇P → □◇P, with bilateral companion ¬◇P → □¬◇P. Both directions matter; the bilateral reading fixed in [§2.1.2](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-2) carries through here.

That conditional marks the work still to be done. The structural ground of possibility *is* what Reality *consists in*, but its invariance across modal evaluation is not assumed here. The Bottleneck ([§2.1.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-5)) and the Transition Closure ([§2.1.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-6)) test whether any candidate alternative can fall outside it. This section fixes the ground to which modal status answers and establishes a separate point: the modal frame is necessarily *occupied* on both sides. Occupancy keeps the frame from being vacuous; the later arguments earn its invariance.

::: {.argument}
**Bilateral Self-Sustenance** · *The Positive Direction*

1. Let ⊤ abbreviate any logical truth.

1. At every world, ⊤ obtains.

1. Whatever obtains at a world is possible relative to the fixed domain of real possibilities.

1. So ⊤ is possible at every world: □◇⊤. Therefore necessarily something is possible: □∃P: ◇P.

:::

The performative version remains available: the act of denying that anything is possible is actual, and therefore possible. But the formal proof needs no move from the content of a supposition to its possibility; ⊤ supplies the positive witness directly.

::: {.argument}
**Bilateral Self-Sustenance** · *The Negative Direction*

1. Let ⊥ abbreviate any contradiction, Q∧¬Q.

1. At no world does ⊥ obtain.

1. So ⊥ is impossible at every world: □¬◇⊥.

1. Therefore necessarily something is impossible: □∃P: ¬◇P.

:::

The two directions rest on different grounds. Logical truth secures the positive pole; noncontradiction secures the negative pole. Neither direction depends on S5, and neither moves from conceivability to real possibility.

Together they establish one result.

::: {.lemma}
**Bilateral Self-Sustenance of Modal Structure** · **L1** · *Lemma toward Necessary Possibility*

Necessarily something is possible, and necessarily something is impossible: both poles of the modal structure are necessarily occupied, not merely kept from going empty. (□∃P: ◇P) ∧ (□∃P: ¬◇P).


:::

The bilateral frame also governs the derivative statuses. Necessity, contingency, and actuality are not independent additions to possibility and impossibility; each is intelligible only within the same frame. A necessary proposition is one whose failure is impossible; a contingent proposition is possible while its negation is possible; an actual proposition is true of the realized configuration. The lemma does not yet show that the contingent status is occupied in every world, or even supply a particular contingent proposition. It fixes the grammar within which that further question can be asked.

Three limits govern how the lemma may be used. The first is a dependency. The canonical proof depends on the global reading of real possibility defended in §[§2.1.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-4)–2.1.5. Transition Closure does not replace that premise: it supplies a narrower S5-independent closure on the onset of Change under structural accessibility. Chapter 3 rebuilds the necessity of direction, difference, and bearer at role-resolution without S5, but it does not independently recover proposition-wise □◇C across silent worlds (worlds with no thinker to token a denial; [§3.1.3](convergence.html#sec-3-1-3)). The dependencies are therefore complementary rather than interchangeable.[^2-1-3-s5-pointers]

The second is a matter of scope. The proof's modal invariance is over the structural conditions that fix modal status, not over the transworld existence of individuals. Neither Barcan formula is load-bearing here, and the quantified modal logic in use neither requires nor forbids constant domains. The closest contemporary view that runs S5 and modal invariance into a substantive quantifier thesis is Williamson's necessitism, which extends necessity to every existent. The present argument shares the invariance and diverges on the scope: necessity attaches to T∧S∧Φ as the structural condition on modal status, not to every individual that occupies it. The divergence point is engaged at [§4.4.6](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-6); the in-chapter scope statement is at [§2.8.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-8-5).

The third concerns grounding. Modal invariance is a shared theorem with the pluriverse account (Lewis's plenitude of concrete possible worlds also yields S5) but the explanatory ground differs. The pluriverse grounds invariance in the completeness of the world-collection; the present account grounds it in what structural incapacity consists in. The Transition Closure ([§2.1.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-6)) brings out the difference: on the pluriverse view, worlds have their change-incapacity essentially; on the present view, structural incapacity is constitutive. Both groundings are engaged at [§4.4.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-1) (Lewis's plenitude) and [§4.3.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-3-9) (structural realism).

*What the Lemma establishes.* The lemma establishes non-vacuity, not proposition-wise modal invariance. The frame necessarily contains at least one possibility and at least one impossibility. It does not yet show that whatever is possible is necessarily possible or that whatever is impossible is necessarily impossible. The axiomatic derivation ([§2.1.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-4)), the Bottleneck's fixed-domain defense ([§2.1.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-5)), and the Transition Closure ([§2.1.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-6)) earn that stronger invariance claim. Occupancy and invariance therefore remain distinct: this lemma supplies the first; the arguments that follow supply the second.

[^2-1-3-invariance-scope]: The invariance is over real / metaphysical modal status (whether P obtains in Reality) not over what remains ideally conceivable under a primary intension or what is epistemically open. The two-dimensional pressure on the invariance claim is engaged at [§4.1.2](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-2).

[^2-1-3-s5-pointers]: The Reverse-Lift diagnostic at [§3.5.4](convergence.html#sec-3-5-4) marks exactly what Chapter 3 reaches without S5 and where □◇C remains upstream. The objections to global modal invariance are met in Chapter 4: [§4.1.4](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-4) takes up Humean contingency, [§4.4.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-9) handles modal collapse, [§4.4.6](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-6) engages Williamson’s necessitism, and [§4.4.8](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-8) takes up the refusal of bilateral invariance.

### 2.1.4 Modal Stability {#sec-2-1-4}

Modal Stability follows once real possibility is evaluated over one fixed domain rather than over a different horizon at each world. This section states that dependency formally.

Let W be the complete domain of worlds Reality permits: the total range of real possibilities. For any proposition P:

- ◇P means that P is true at some world in W.
- □P means that P is true at every world in W.

The domain W is fixed across evaluation. Moving the point at which a formula is evaluated does not replace Reality's range of possibilities with another range. This is the substantive globality claim; the Bottleneck ([§2.1.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-5)) defends it against world-relative alternatives.

::: {.argument}
**Modal Stability** · *The Fixed-Domain Derivation*

1. *T.* If □P, then P is true at every world in W. The world of evaluation is a member of W, so P is true there: □P → P.

1. *S4.* If □P, then P is true throughout W. Since every world evaluates necessity over that same W, □P is true at every world: □P → □□P.

1. *B.* If P is true at a world w, then w itself witnesses ◇P. Since every world evaluates possibility over the same W containing w, ◇P is true at every world: P → □◇P.

1. T, S4, and B over the normal modal base yield S5. In particular, whatever is possible is necessarily possible: ◇P → □◇P.

1. The bilateral companion follows over the same fixed domain: if no world in W makes P true, that absence is unchanged at every point of evaluation. ¬◇P → □¬◇P.

:::

The derivation does not use Temporality, Spatiality, or Physicality, and therefore does not assume the later conclusion that those Conditions hold in every world. It uses only the meaning of real possibility fixed in [§1.2.1](groundwork.html#sec-1-2-1): a modal determination Reality settles over its complete range of permitted ways. The Conditions will later be derived as the content that range necessarily realizes; they are not a premise in fixing the range's globality.

::: {.corollary}
**Necessity entails Possibility** · **R1** · *Result of the T-Axiom and the Actuality–Possibility Principle*

Whatever is necessary is possible. □P → ◇P.


:::

The result composes T (□P → P) with actuality implying possibility (P → ◇P). Contraposed, ¬◇P → ¬□P: what is not possible is not necessary.

The fixed-domain reading is equivalent, in ordinary Kripke semantics, to universal accessibility within W. Kripke [-@kripke1963] supplies the model-theoretic form; Williamson [-@williamson2013] defends S5 for metaphysical necessity. The present account identifies the philosophical commitment beneath that form: *real possibility* ranges over Reality's possibilities as a whole, not over a local horizon owned by each world.

This leaves a precise point of contestation. A critic may insist that possibility is fundamentally world-relative, with each world carrying its own accessible domain. That is not a counterexample inside the present operator; it is a rival account of what ◇ means. The Bottleneck takes up that rival directly and asks whether local reachability and real possibility have been conflated.

*What is established.* Given one fixed domain W of real possibilities, T, S4, B, the Euclidean principle, and its bilateral companion follow without appealing to the Triconditions. S5 is therefore downstream of global real possibility, not upstream of the Necessity of Nature.[^2-1-4-s5-derivation-ch4]

[^2-1-4-s5-derivation-ch4]: World-relative and rival-domain readings are engaged through Lewis ([§4.4.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-1)), Williamson ([§4.4.6](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-6)), modal collapse ([§4.4.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-9)), Sider ([§4.4.7](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-7)), and the source-of-possibility question ([§4.1.10](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-10)).

### 2.1.5 The S5 Bottleneck {#sec-2-1-5}

Modal Stability ([§2.1.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-4)) derives S5 from one substantive commitment: real possibility ranges over a single fixed domain W, the complete range of ways Reality permits. The Bottleneck's job is to defend that globality against the strongest alternative, not to establish in advance that every world instantiates T, S, and Φ.

*The local-horizon objection.* A critic may hold that φ is possible from one world w but not from another world w′ because each world carries its own accessibility horizon. On that semantics, ◇ is indexed to a world-relative relation: ◇₍w₎φ may hold while ◇₍w′₎φ fails.

The reply is a distinction between two modalities. World-relative reachability can represent what can develop from a state, what laws local to a world permit, or which nodes a model connects. Real possibility, fixed at [§1.2.1](groundwork.html#sec-1-2-1), asks a different question: whether φ is among the ways Reality permits at all. Let W be that complete range. If some world in W makes φ true, then φ is really possible. Evaluating that same claim at another member of W does not replace W with a new Reality. The witness remains in the fixed domain, so ◇φ remains true throughout W and □◇φ follows.

This is not an exemption-by-definition. It states the exact philosophical choice the operator carries. If a critic uses ◇ for local reachability, the critic has changed the subject from global metaphysical possibility to a relative modality. Such relative modalities are legitimate, but their variation does not show that *real possibility* varies. It shows that reachability from a node and membership in Reality's total possibility-domain are different relations.

::: {.argument}
**The Fixed-Domain Bottleneck** · *from global real possibility to Necessary Possibility*

1. W is the complete domain of worlds Reality permits.

1. ◇P means that P is true at some world in W.

1. If ◇P, some witness world u in W makes P true.

1. Every world w in W evaluates real possibility over that same W, so u remains a witness at w.

1. Therefore ◇P is true at every world in W: □◇P.

:::

The proof is schematic and content-neutral. It says nothing about which propositions are possible and imports no claim that T, S, or Φ already hold necessarily. That separation removes the circular line of argument in which the Conditions would be used to derive S5 and S5 then used to necessitate the Conditions.

*Concrete and primitive worlds.* Lewisian modal realism may treat worlds as concrete and mutually isolated; primitivism may treat modal facts as ungrounded. Neither ontology by itself changes the operator. If the collection of worlds is the range of metaphysical possibilities, quantification over that collection is global even when its members are causally isolated. A theorist who instead assigns each world a private metaphysical possibility-domain owes an account of whether those domains are themselves jointly possible. If they are, their union supplies the global W at which the present operator ranges; if they are not, the alleged variation never enters one shared modal comparison.

A separate structural consequence matters downstream, though it is not a premise of Necessary Possibility.

::: {.lemma}
**Parasitic Negation** · **L2** · *Lemma toward Negation Seal*

Let D be one of T, S, or Φ. A claim that D begins from its own absence presupposes D in the proposed onset: a first moment requires temporal order, a first placing requires positional structure, and a first production requires a bearer across the transition. Domain-internal absence may be coherent; emergence of the domain from domain-external absence is not.


:::

The distinction is between absence *within* a domain and onset *of* the domain. “No event occurs during an interval” is internal to Temporality; “Temporality first appears where no temporal order obtains” asks temporal order to precede itself. “Nothing occupies this place” is internal to Spatiality; “the first place is placed where no positional structure obtains” asks placement to precede its domain. The same form applies to production and Φ.

::: {.corollary}
**Negation Seal** · **R2** · *Result of L2*

A candidate history in which D emerges from domain-external ¬D is incoherent. Either the negation is domain-internal, in which case D remains instantiated, or the proposed onset already uses D. No third onset is available.


:::

The scope is exact. Parasitic Negation rules out onset from domain-external absence. It does not by itself show that every possible world instantiates D, and it does not derive proposition-wise modal invariance. Transition Closure ([§2.1.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-6)) develops its consequence for C-status under an explicit structural-accessibility premise. The Necessity of Nature is established later by Necessary Possibility, the Cartesian witness, and the Structural Requirement — not smuggled into this Bottleneck.

*What is foreclosed.* A proposition cannot be really possible at one world and not really possible at another when “really possible” quantifies over the same total domain W at both. World-relative reachability may vary, but it is a different modality. The remaining disagreement is therefore clean: whether metaphysical possibility is global in the sense fixed at [§1.2.1](groundwork.html#sec-1-2-1). Chapter 4 engages rival answers rather than treating them as incoherent by stipulation.[^2-1-5-bottleneck-ch4]

[^2-1-5-bottleneck-ch4]: Concrete modal realism and rival accessibility structures are engaged at [§4.4.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-1); invariant-domain and necessitist readings at [§4.4.6](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-6); primitivist and structuralist alternatives at [§4.4.7](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-7); refusals of bilateral invariance at [§4.4.8](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-8)–[§4.4.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-9); and the source of possibility at [§4.1.10](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-10).

### 2.1.6 The Transition Closure {#sec-2-1-6}

The S5 forward inference ([§2.1.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-4)) packages modal invariance into its cleanest form, but it borrows the cross-world invariance it turns on from the Bottleneck ([§2.1.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-5)) rather than generating it. Parasitic Negation ([§2.1.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-5)) yields a separate closure concerning Change.

Its temporal core is unconditional: a state in which Change is impossible cannot produce Change, because that production would itself be a change. Its modal extension is conditional on the structural reading of accessibility used here. The result is not a theorem of bare Kripke semantics, on which accessibility may be only an abstract relation between nodes. Here accessibility marks a structurally available alternative within the same Reality. Under that explicit reading, an alternative differing in C-status must be structurally reachable as an alternative, and the required connection is what the Negation Seal rules out.

Let "changeless" abbreviate ¬◇C; let P(¬C, C) abbreviate "a changeless state produces Change."

::: {.argument}
**Transition Closure** · *Spelling Out the Closure Across Accessibility*

1. *Negation Seal.* A changeless state cannot produce Change. ¬P(¬C, C). ([§2.1.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-5))

1. Any transition from ¬◇C into ◇C would itself be a Change.

1. From (1) and (2): a ¬◇C state cannot host the transition that would carry it into ◇C.

1. *Structural-accessibility premise.* An alternative is accessible here only if it is structurally available as a way the same Reality could be. If two alternatives differ in C-status, their structural availability must connect the no-Change state to the Change-permitting state.

1. From (3) and (4): under structural accessibility, ¬◇C is closed. Every structurally accessible alternative to a ¬◇C state is itself ¬◇C.

1. **Transition Closure.** The conditional closure therefore holds without assuming S5: ¬◇C → □¬◇C, hence □(¬◇C → □¬◇C). The box ranges over structural accessibility; no claim is made here about a bare abstract accessibility relation.

:::

The result restates that conclusion and reads it in both directions at once, temporal and modal.

::: {.corollary}
**Transition Closure** · **R3** · *Result of L2*

A state that lacks the possibility of Change cannot produce or transition into a Change-permitting state. Under structural accessibility, every alternative available from it therefore remains at ¬◇C. The temporal conclusion is unconditional: no possible history begins with Change impossible and later acquires it. The modal conclusion is conditional on structural accessibility: no ¬◇C alternative is structurally accessible from a ◇C alternative, or conversely. The result does not by itself exclude an isolated ¬◇C world under a bare abstract semantics. The ∅ Reductio at [§2.7.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-7-4) addresses the empty alternative, not an isolated structured world in which Change is impossible. □(¬◇C → □¬◇C).


:::

The structural-accessibility reading carries step 4. An alternative is not merely a listed node: it is a way the same Reality could be, and its availability must be answerable to the relation that makes it structurally reachable from the state in question. Where the proposed alternative differs from ¬◇C by allowing Change, its availability requires the transition step 1 rules out. On a bare abstract-relation reading the inference would not go through; the closure is explicitly not offered as a theorem of such semantics.

What the closure establishes on its own is a structural fact about ¬◇C: it does not connect to its own absence. The Humean who posits brute emergence (the capacity for change appearing without any mechanism, from a state that lacks it) has not bypassed this point. Brute emergence is itself a transition from absence to presence, and a transition is Change.

So the closure rules out the prior-changelessness picture and nothing wider. It neither establishes that every world permits Change nor rules out an isolated ¬◇C world under an unrelated accessibility semantics. Nor does the later ∅ analysis close that gap: it concerns the coherence of the empty alternative, not a second derivation of Necessary Possibility.

*What closes.* The Transition Closure is an S5-independent closure on C-status, conditional in its modal form on the structural-accessibility premise made explicit above. A reader who rejects S5 while granting that premise has a reason to reject the emergence of Change from a capacityless state. They do not thereby receive proposition-wise □◇C. Modal Persistence and Modal Invariance ([§2.1.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-7)) are therefore governed by the fixed-domain semantics of Necessary Possibility; Transition Closure remains an auxiliary onset argument. Its exact result is the narrower one its name records: a ¬◇C state cannot host its own exit.[^2-1-6-transition-closure-ch4]

[^2-1-6-transition-closure-ch4]: The claim that ¬◇C is closed under accessibility meets several objections in Chapter 4, the brute-emergence reading of the Humean chief among them. The Humean denial of necessary connection is the brute-emergence position the closure rules out ([§4.1.4](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-4)); the changeless-world picture supplies the prior state the closure forecloses ([§4.2.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-1)); emergent-time accounts ask whether the transition into change can be staged from outside ([§4.2.3](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-3)); and dialetheist refusals ask whether ¬◇C can both hold and fail at the transition ([§4.4.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-9)).

### 2.1.7 Two Readings {#sec-2-1-7}

The Necessary Possibility Theorem has two readings because the fixed domain of real possibility can be indexed in two ways. The theorem itself is one result: all modal evaluation ranges over the same complete domain W of real possibilities (§[§1.2.1](groundwork.html#sec-1-2-1), 2.1.4–2.1.5). It does not rest on a separate w′ derivation or on Transition Closure.

*Modal Persistence, the diachronic reading.* A later time does not create a new domain of real possibilities. What becomes locally achievable, ceases to be locally achievable, or is never actualized concerns occasions and configurations; it does not add or remove members of W. A possibility may lack an occasion at a time without lapsing in modal status.

*Modal Invariance, the cross-world reading.* The same point holds across worlds. A witness to ◇P is a member of W, and every world evaluates real possibility over W. Thus ◇P → □◇P; if no member of W witnesses P, ¬◇P → □¬◇P.

The two readings are not two causal stories about structural Conditions changing or persisting. They are two indices of one global semantic fact: temporal changes and world-relative accessibility relations do not replace the complete domain that real possibility quantifies over.

Plantinga [-@plantinga1974b] develops modal invariance for essentialist claims about individuals. The present theorem generalizes the result to real modal status and grounds it in the fixed global domain of possibility. A critic may instead use a world-relative modality with varying accessibility horizons; that is a different operator, not a counterexample within ◇.

*What binds.* The modal architecture is globally stable: whatever modal status a proposition bears in the complete domain W, that status is invariant under evaluation at any member of W. Local opportunity remains local; real possibility is global.[^2-1-7-two-readings-ch4]

[^2-1-7-two-readings-ch4]: The global and relative readings of modality are pressed in Chapter 4: Williamson ([§4.4.6](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-6)), Lewis ([§4.4.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-1)), modal collapse ([§4.4.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-9)), and the source-of-possibility question ([§4.1.10](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-10)).

### 2.1.8 Candidate-Ground Convergence {#sec-2-1-8}

Whatever the ground of existence is (divine creation, quantum vacuum, Mathematical Platonism, brute contingency) it has to be possible. Otherwise it grounds nothing. And whatever is possible is necessarily possible. That is what S5 says: ◇P → □◇P. The theorem converges on every candidate, and none passes through it unchanged.

Many candidates are proposed as necessary rather than merely possible, and for those the discipline tightens: a necessary ground holds in every possible world. None of that settles what the ground is; it fixes the modal discipline any candidate must meet.

So ask what the candidate has to instantiate in order to do grounding work. If it hosts succession, distinction, and exchange (if it is temporal, spatial, and physical) then it is not yet an alternative to Nature but a candidate that satisfies Nature's structural profile under another vocabulary. And if it does not host succession, distinction, or exchange, then it loses the determinacy required to be a ground at all ([§2.8.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-8-6)). The pressure on every proposed necessary ground is therefore this: either it resolves into the structure of Reality, or it must explain how a ground with no T, no S, and no Φ can still ground anything.

This applies equally to apophatic positions: Plotinus' One above being, the Eckhartian Godhead beyond God, Buddhist śūnyatā framed as beyond all categories, contemporary 'ground beyond ground' moves. Such positions say something content-bearing about a putative ground: that it is the source of what has being, that it is real in some sense rigorous enough to ground other things, that it stands in some relation to what it grounds. To say even that much is to grant the ground enough determinacy to bear a relation to what it grounds, and determinacy plus relation is structure under another name. If the apophatic move is consistent and the 'beyond being' really is beyond all the Conditions (no Temporality, no Spatiality, no Physicality, no determinacy at all) then it is the no-content case, not a ground: nothing determinate remains to bear the grounding relation ([§2.8.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-8-6)). The apophatic ground either retains enough determinacy to ground (confirming the structure under negation-laden vocabulary) or surrenders all determinacy (collapsing into the no-content case). There is no third position from which a 'ground beyond' can do the work the apophatic tradition asks of it.

The universality admits no exemptions, not even the objection to S5 itself. "It is possible S5 is wrong" is a proposition like any other. If S5 holds, the claim that S5 is possibly wrong is necessarily possible, but possibility is not refutation, and an actual demonstration is still required. Nor is the objection self-undermining: necessary possibility is not necessary truth. This is not an independent argument for S5; it is what S5's closure looks like from the inside.

The fixed-domain derivation earns proposition-wise modal invariance through Modal Stability ([§2.1.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-4)) and the Bottleneck ([§2.1.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-5)). Transition Closure ([§2.1.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-6)) is narrower: an auxiliary argument about the onset of Change under structural accessibility, not another derivation of S5.

A contemporary precedent points at the same convergence from a different direction. Van Hamme [@vanHamme2025a; @vanHamme2025b] argues that modal logic is jurisdictionally confined to logical-analytic and modal-structural necessity, and that classical theism's claim of a necessary personal being asks the modal apparatus to certify a class of necessity (existential) it cannot reach. Van Hamme reads this as a defeater for the classical move; the present argument reads it as the same closure seen from outside the structural ground. The class of necessity modal logic *can* legitimately deliver is precisely the class T ∧ S ∧ Φ occupies. Where van Hamme stops at the jurisdictional limit, the structural derivation ([§2.1.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-5), [§2.1.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-6)) shows that what fills the legitimate class is structural Reality itself. Same boundary, two sides of it.

*What converges.* The reader who proposes an alternate ground can take the same path. The ground is either temporal, spatial, and physical (in which case it confirms the structure of Reality) or it is not, in which case the burden is to show how it remains a ground rather than the no-content case under another vocabulary.[^2-1-8-candidate-ground-ch4]

[^2-1-8-candidate-ground-ch4]: The objections to the candidate-ground convergence are taken up in Chapters 4 and 5. The apophatic positions (Plotinus' One, the Eckhartian Godhead, śūnyatā, and the contemporary 'ground beyond ground') fall under classical simplicity and the apophatic-theological tradition, the principal target of the determinacy-plus-relation argument ([§5.2](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-2)). The contrasting cataphatic line is Plantinga's necessary personal being ([§5.1.7](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-7)), with Swinburne on personal-explanation grounds ([§5.1.4](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-4)) and idealism on whether the ground is mental rather than structural ([§4.3.5](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-3-5)). The van Hamme jurisdictional reading is engaged directly under the jurisdictional-limits treatment ([§5.1.7](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-7)), and Lewis raises whether alternative grounds can be hosted by plenitude rather than by structure ([§4.4.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-1)).

### 2.1.9 What Necessity Transfer Needs {#sec-2-1-9}

The modal ontological argument turns on the S5 transfer from possible necessity to necessity: ◇□P → □P. Within the present account, that transfer follows from the fixed global domain W of real possibilities. It does not follow merely because an attempted rejection linguistically presupposes the framework.

Like the Euclidean principle before it ([§2.1.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-4)), the transfer is schematic. Grant that a proposition is necessary at some member of W. Because every world evaluates necessity over the same W, the proposition is necessary at every member: ◇□P → □P. The inference does not turn on whose proposition P is.

A critic may reject this account only by offering a different semantics of real possibility — one on which necessity is evaluated over genuinely different global domains rather than over W. Merely using modal language to deny S5 does not refute the fixed-domain analysis, but neither does it make denial incoherent by itself. It states a competing modal theory that Chapter 4 evaluates in detail.

The theist is therefore bound if the fixed-domain account is accepted, and the modal ontological argument itself supplies a particularly clear instance: ◇□G → □G. Whether that transfer delivers a theistic conclusion, and what it costs to resist it, is not adjudicated here; the full engagement with Plantinga's argument belongs to Chapter 5 ([§5.1.7](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-7)).

*What inverts.* The move the tradition reserved for crowning a necessary being is a structural consequence of global real possibility. It binds every claim evaluated within W, the theist included; it is not a verdict directed against any claimant.

### 2.1.10 Necessary Possibility {#sec-2-1-10}

Real possibility ranges over one fixed domain W, the complete set of worlds Reality permits, and that fixed domain yields a single result: modal status is invariant across every point of evaluation, a result the rest of the chapter relies on.

::: {.argument}
**Necessary Possibility** · *The Derivation*

1. *Modal Exhaustiveness.* Every contentful proposition receives one of the two classical verdicts: ◇P or ¬◇P. ([§2.1.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-1))

1. *Global real possibility.* W is the complete domain of worlds Reality permits. ◇P means truth at some member of W; □P means truth at every member. ([§1.2.1](groundwork.html#sec-1-2-1), [§2.1.3](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-3))

1. *Fixed-domain invariance.* Every world evaluates real possibility over that same W. A witness world for P therefore remains a witness at every point of evaluation. ([§2.1.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-4))

1. *The Bottleneck.* A world-relative accessibility horizon may vary, but that is local reachability, not the global metaphysical possibility fixed by W. No variation in local reachability changes membership in W. ([§2.1.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-5))

1. *Bilateral Self-Sustenance (L1).* Logical truth supplies a necessary possibility-witness and contradiction a necessary impossibility-witness, so the fixed frame is non-vacuously occupied on both sides. (□∃P: ◇P) ∧ (□∃P: ¬◇P). ([§2.1.3](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-3))

:::

Together, these results close on a single conclusion:

::: {.theorem}
**Necessary Possibility** · **T1** · *Theorem 1*

Whatever is possible is necessarily possible; whatever is impossible is necessarily impossible. Modal status is invariant because every point of evaluation ranges over the same total domain of real possibilities. ◇P → □◇P, with bilateral companion ¬◇P → □¬◇P.


:::

The theorem is schematic. It does not say that anything in particular is possible; it says that once a proposition has a real modal status, changing the evaluation point does not change the global domain over which that status is evaluated. The Cartesian witness supplies the substantive input in [§2.2](the-argument.html#sec-2-2).

The derivation is also non-circular with the later Necessity of Nature. No step assumes that T, S, or Φ holds in every world. The fixed-domain theorem concerns the quantificational scope of real possibility; §[§2.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-4)–2.5 later identify and necessitate the structural content every world in that domain must realize.

The name is conventional. *Necessary Possibility* names the positive S5 form, while the theorem is bilateral: absence of a witness from W is as invariant as presence of one.

*What is established.* Real possibility is global, modal status is rigid across W, and both verdicts are necessarily instantiated. S5 is derived from fixed-domain metaphysical modality rather than from the Triconditions it later helps necessitate.

## 2.2 Cartesian Certainty {#sec-2-2}

This section supplies the proof's input, not its conclusion. The S5 pipeline of [§2.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-1) closed with a conditional and no antecedent discharged: whatever is possible is necessarily possible (the Necessary Possibility Theorem, [§2.1.10](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-10)). Nothing has yet been shown to be possible. The theorem needs exactly one input: ◇C, that change is really possible. And change is not merely possible but actual, since the reading of this sentence instantiates it. Nor is the input deniable. Trying to deny change performs it.

::: {.premise}
**Cartesian Certainty** · **P2** · *Premise 2*

Change is really possible. No denial can escape it: the act of doubting that anything changes is itself a change, from not-doubting to doubting. ◇C.


:::

The certainty is Cartesian in a precise sense. The witness is the *Cogito*'s structural shadow: any attempt to doubt that change occurs is itself a change, a transition from not-doubting to doubting, performed across a real interval, hosted by a persistent doubter. The doubter here is a functional role: the state constituting doubt is structurally distinct from its absence, and that structural difference is the change the witness requires. The doubt refutes itself in its own performance: no denial of change can be completed without instantiating it. That is Cartesian certainty for the possibility of change, in one exact grade: the performative inescapability of the structural transition, self-defeating to deny, not the phenomenal indubitability the term can suggest. "Cartesian" marks the *Cogito* on the performative reading taken up at [§2.2.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-2-1), not an introspective luminosity of the doubting.

Two limits hold that grade in place. Phenomenal character is not the datum, and the witness does not depend on it (that pressure is taken up at [§4.3.2](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-3-2)). And the change instantiated is intrinsic state change of the doubting system, not duration of time or causal direction per se: what the witness establishes is that change is sufficient to instantiate the structural Conditions, not that temporal structure cannot proceed without intrinsic change, which is Shoemaker's freeze argument and is engaged at [§4.2.2](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-2).[^2-2-0-change-witness-ch4]

The performative catch is the *Cogito*'s shape redirected: *Cogito Ergo Muto*. The argument is given in full at [§2.2.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-2-1), where change is shown to be actual and certain at three depths — empirically, performatively, and structurally — under the *Cogito*-style closure of [§1.3](groundwork.html#sec-1-3) that no skeptical scenario can undermine.

The input then does its work in two directions. First, it does not lapse once secured: fed into the Necessary Possibility Theorem ([§2.1.10](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-10)), ◇C carries to its necessitated form, □◇C: what is possible is possible in every world constituted by modal structure. Second, the certainty reaches past experience to whatever grounds it: the extension from the act of doubting to any ground that could host it is carried at [§2.2.2](the-argument.html#sec-2-2-2) by three independent lines — level-invariance, the Triconditional Cross-Entailment, and the Encoding Dilemma, whose result, Constitutive Instantiation, is proved at [§2.6.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-7).

The argument extends a defended tradition. @hintikka1962 read Descartes' *sum* as performed rather than inferred: the *Cogito*'s force lies in the fact that any denial of one's existence re-establishes it in the act of denying. @apel1980 and @habermas1983 extended the move to the presuppositions of argumentation itself. @stroud1968 and @taylor1978 formalized the general pattern: an X is unavoidable if every possible denial of X requires X for its formulation. What is new here is the target: not the presuppositions of reasoning in general but the structural conditions of any state of affairs being the case, regardless of whether anyone argues about it.

Stroud's own objection sharpens the stakes. Transcendental arguments, taken alone, establish only what must be presupposed for experience or assertion to occur. What entitles the move from a fact about the act of denial to a conclusion about mind-independent reality? Nothing — so long as the performative line stands alone. The reply is a pairing. The performative line (this section) shows that the act of denial or conceiving is itself structurally conditioned: anyone running the denial uses what it rejects. The constitutive-definition line ([§1.4](groundwork.html#sec-1-4)) carries the metaphysical claim: the Conditions are what it is for any state of affairs to be the case — constitutive of its obtaining, not its subject matter. Neither move alone closes the gap. Cognitive performance alone does not defeat the ideal conceivability of a structureless scenario, and the constitutive definitions alone leave the performance certainty unanchored. The two together do.[^2-2-0-cogito-illusion-ch4]

[^2-2-0-cogito-illusion-ch4]: [§4.3.2](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-3-2) engages the Ch 4 objections that the cognitive performance the *Cogito* presupposes is itself illusory or eliminable; [§4.3.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-3-1) takes up the related objection that consciousness as substrate stands outside structural exhaustion, the hard problem of consciousness. The input secures the possibility of change without itself answering the hard-problem pressure, which is carried forward rather than discharged here.

[^2-2-0-change-witness-ch4]: The [§4.2](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2) cluster engages the Ch 4 objections targeting the change-witness itself: [§4.2.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-1) takes up changeless-ground accounts that would refuse the witness, and [§4.2.2](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-2) handles Shoemaker's argument that the temporal structure can hold without change.

### 2.2.1 Change Is Actual {#sec-2-2-1}

At the level of ordinary experience, change is not a hypothesis; it is the most immediate and universal feature of observation. Every perception presupposes change: to perceive is to receive a succession of sensory states (succession). Every measurement presupposes relational displacement: to measure is to compare positions across a relational interval (distinction). Every experiment presupposes causal transmission: to intervene is to transmit causal influence from apparatus to subject (exchange).

The sciences do not discover that change occurs. They presuppose it as the condition of possibility for scientific inquiry itself, and in doing so presuppose all three structural requirements of any transition simultaneously. Even the denier of change must formulate the denial, a process that unfolds in time, occupies a position, and persists long enough to reach its conclusion.

This empirical certainty is the starting point but not the foundation. It is logically possible (if not coherently imaginable) that our empirical experience is systematically deceived. The foundation of P2 lies deeper, at the level where deception itself cannot reach.

Even granting radical skepticism in its strongest form (the scenario @descartes1641 deploys in the *Meditations*, that our experience may be a simulation, a dream, the product of a deceiving demon, or a systematic illusion of any other kind) the possibility of change cannot be coherently denied. The denial is self-refuting at the level of its own performance.

To think is to undergo a succession of mental states: the state of not-yet-having-thought this thought, and the state of having-thought it. To doubt is to transition from a state of not-yet-doubting to a state of doubting. To process this argument is to move through a sequence of propositions, each one replacing its predecessor as the object of attention. Each of these acts just is change in the sense defined in [§1.3](groundwork.html#sec-1-3): one state, then another. To deny that change occurs is to transition from not-denying to denying, a cognitive succession that instantiates what the denial contests. One cannot deny change without undergoing it. The trying is the change. The denial of ◇C cannot be completed without instantiating the very possibility it denies. This is the *Cogito* structure applied to change rather than existence — the move this book names *Cogito Ergo Muto*.

The oldest denial of ◇C aims at this target. *Zeno's paradoxes* of motion — the Dichotomy and the Achilles, which cut any passage into endlessly many sub-passages that could never be completed, and the Arrow, which freezes flight into instants at none of which anything moves (all transmitted in Aristotle's *Physics* VI.9 [@aristotle1984]) — conclude that motion, and so change, is illusory. The witness does not adjudicate the paradoxes on their own ground; it refuses their conclusion and names the hidden premise that made it seem forced. What is secured here is bare succession: one state, then another ([§1.3](groundwork.html#sec-1-3)), which commits neither to completing an infinite task nor to finding motion within a durationless instant.

Against the Dichotomy, the endless task-list is not found in the passage but imposed on it — by stopping to mark each halfway point — and stopping to mark is not the passage but its interruption. A reader who marks the midpoint of this sentence, then the midpoint of what remains, and again, has stopped reading in order to measure; the reader who reads reaches the period. The marking that generates the regress is itself one state after another, so the objection is carried out by the very succession it concludes cannot occur.

Against the Arrow, that the arrow fills exactly its own length at an instant is not rest but what any extended thing does at any instant, moving or still: it registers the arrow's extension and its persistence at that time (Spatiality and Physicality) and is silent about succession (Temporality), which is constituted across instants, not within one. The Arrow reads rest off the mere standing presence of the bearer, mistaking the absence of motion within a slice for its absence across the slices. What the reader who finishes this sentence has just done, the Eleatic says cannot be done — and the finishing is the refutation.[^2-2-1-zeno-paradoxes]

@hintikka1962 reads the *Cogito* as performative rather than inferential: the certainty of *I am* does not follow from *I think* as a logical inference but is existentially inseparable from the act of thinking; the attempted denial of one's own existence is self-defeating in the performing, not in the reasoning. The present argument is the performative reading redirected. Where Hintikka's *Cogito* catches the denier in the act of existing, this one catches the denier in the act of undergoing change. Existence and change are not the same target, but the closure is the same move, and Hintikka's analysis clarifies why it is not question-begging: the closure does not derive its content from a premise the denier might refuse; it derives it from the act the denier cannot refuse without ceasing to act at all.

Descartes established that the act of doubting proves the existence of a doubting subject. This argument establishes the actuality of Change in the act of doubting.

What the performative catch establishes is *Change*, and only that. The act also displays distinctions — a doubting thought, what is doubted, and the standpoint from which the doubt is made — but this section does not treat that distinction by itself as a completed proof of Spatiality. Nor does the act alone complete the proof of Physicality merely by requiring a bearer of thought. Those stronger conclusions are earned where the book argues that genuine transition requires directed ordering, traversable distinction, and persistence: the Structural Requirement ([§2.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-4)), the level-invariance line ([§2.2.2](the-argument.html#sec-2-2-2)), and the later cross-entailment arguments. The witness supplies the actual Change those arguments require; it does not silently replace them.

The deceiving demon, the simulation architect, the dreaming mind: none of these escape the argument, because each must itself undergo causally structured succession to operate. The level-invariance step here (that the structural Conditions hold at the level of the deceiver as well as the level of the deceived) is developed at [§2.2.2](the-argument.html#sec-2-2-2) (which establishes level-independence across putative ontological levels); the present section uses it as a closing example, while the level-invariance argument carries the argumentative weight.

The skeptical scenarios that are meant to undermine the certainty of ◇C each presuppose it as their own condition of possibility. The Cartesian certainty of ◇C is therefore not merely empirical certainty that survives scrutiny. It is epistemic inescapability: there is no coherent epistemic position (no possible standpoint of doubt, denial, or inquiry) from which ◇C can be coherently rejected. Any position from which the rejection is attempted instantiates the possibility it attempts to reject.

The move runs parallel to the epistemic-closure literature [@dretske1970; @nozick1981; @deRose1995] but inverts its direction: rather than running closure forward from known premises to their known consequences, the performative catch runs closure backward from the act of denial to the structural Conditions that act already instantiates.

*The token-level reach.* Any particular act of denial instantiates change. But could "change is not possible" still be true in some world where no one denies it? The token catch does not close that type-level question by itself. The constitutive-definition argument of [§1.4](groundwork.html#sec-1-4) does that work: because the structural roles are fully constitutive of the essences they specify, the token catch is not a coincidence of the denier's situation but a structural feature of the proposition's content. The performative line and the constitutive line are complementary: the first shows that any denial uses what it rejects, the second shows the Conditions are what it is for anything to be the case. This distinguishes the argument from Boghossian's [-@boghossian1998] observation that self-knowledge claims do not ground substantive metaphysical conclusions. The performative catches here do not rest on the subject's self-knowledge. They rest on the structural preconditions of any propositional act, conditions that are constitutive of what propositional content consists in, not merely features of the act of knowing.

What is secured at this point: ◇C, the actuality of change. The Necessary Possibility Theorem ([§2.1.10](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-10)) performs the amplification from ◇C to □◇C; [§2.2.2](the-argument.html#sec-2-2-2) takes up whether the certainty extends from experience to the ground of experience.

[^2-2-1-zeno-paradoxes]: The reading of the subdivisions as *potential* — generated by the act of dividing rather than antecedently completed — is Aristotle's own (*Physics* VIII.8 [@aristotle1984]); the reading of motion as a unity misdescribed when reconstituted from the stationary positions it passes through is Bergson's [@bergson1907]. The formal dissolution of the divisibility paradoxes in the convergent series (½ + ¼ + ⅛ + … = 1) meets them on their own ground; the witness does not need it, since ◇C rides on bare succession rather than the summed continuum.

### 2.2.2 Actuality's Reach {#sec-2-2-2}

The actuality of change is Cartesian-certain ([§2.2.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-2-1)): the act of reading is itself a change, and that experienced change exhibits causally structured succession, relational extension, and causal persistence. What remains is whether those Conditions belong only to experience, or to whatever constitutes its ground.

One distinction governs the extension. At the first pass, T, S, and Φ name roles: directed priority, real differentiation, and a real bearer or realizer. Those roles must not be silently upgraded into clock time, metric extension, or material causation. The general grounding argument establishes the roles. Concrete grounds such as computational substrates may instantiate richer temporal, spatial, and causal types, but that is a further realization claim.

The extension runs through three lines with different scopes: level-invariance establishes the roles any ground must realize; the Triconditional Cross-Entailment governs full Condition-instantiation within change-realizers; and the Encoding Dilemma handles live representational grounds such as simulations. They converge on structured grounding without pretending to be premise-disjoint.

*Level-invariance.* The level-invariance argument is the most fundamental of them. It does not depend on how causal transmission works between levels, or on any particular account of what the ground of experience consists in. It depends only on what any grounding relation structurally requires. For one level of reality to host another (for a substrate to host a simulation, a demon to host a dream, a transcendental subject to host experience) that hosting relation must satisfy three structural Conditions.

A ground must be metaphysically prior to what it grounds. This priority need not be temporal or causal [grounding is standardly atemporal; @fine2012; @schaffer2009], but it must be asymmetric and directed. That establishes the T-role of directed order, not yet temporal succession. Treating metaphysical priority as an instance of clock time would contradict the definition of grounding fixed at [§1.5.5](groundwork.html#sec-1-5-5); the argument needs only the role shared by temporal succession and atemporal dependence.

The ground must also be genuinely distinct from what it grounds. That establishes the S-role of real differentiation, not yet traversable spatial extension. Finally, the grounding fact must obtain: there must be something in which the dependence consists rather than a free-floating description. That establishes the Φ-role of real bearing or realization, not yet persistence across a causal interval. The richer spatial and causal types require their own arguments.

This holds at every level of any possible ontological stack.

::: {.argument}
**The Grounding Conditional** · *The Level-Invariance Line*

1. Any grounding relation R(x,y) requires asymmetric priority (the T-role), real differentiation of x from y (the S-role), and a real fact or realizer in which R obtains (the Φ-role).

1. Whenever R holds, at any level of an ontological stack, those three roles are instantiated at the level of the ground.

1. Therefore any coherent ground of actual change instantiates directed order, differentiation, and bearing: T∧S∧Φ at role-resolution.

1. The line does not by itself identify their concrete types. Temporal succession, spatial extension, and causal persistence require the separate realizer arguments developed later.

:::

Level-invariance therefore secures a role-level extension from experienced structure to any ground of that experience. The unconditional necessity result is reached later, when Necessary Possibility is combined with the Structural Requirement ([§2.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-4)); the ∅ argument removes the purported empty alternative but is not a hidden premise in this extension. What this secures, if the grounding relation is granted, is the extension from certainty within experience to certainty at the level of whatever hosts it. The question is no longer whether change is certain *for us*. Could a ground underwrite that certainty while standing outside the very roles it must exercise to ground anything at all? Level-invariance says no. Nothing here depends on the Triconditional Cross-Entailment or on Constitutive Instantiation. If grounding is real, the Conditions are already in play.

*Causal realization.* Skeptical hypotheses about the ground of experience make the richer, type-level requirement concrete. They also anticipate the Encoding Dilemma below: a substrate that merely *encodes* our world must still instantiate the Conditions in order to host a live experience. Suppose our reality is a simulation running on a computational substrate, the most familiar deflation and the case whose machinery makes the requirement easiest to see. The substrate must execute temporal succession to process the simulation's states (T), differentiate the computational elements that encode distinct positions (S), and contain causally active components whose interactions produce its outputs (Φ). These are what level-invariance requires of any simulation-hosting substrate in any possible world, not only our own. A substrate that lacks them does not run a different kind of simulation; it runs none at all, because simulation is a causal process requiring temporal succession, relational differentiation, and a medium of causal transmission.

The empirical particulars of *our* computational substrates instantiate those structural Conditions; they are not the Conditions themselves. Hardware has locational structure (chips, memory, buses, racks); energy cycles; processors obey conservation constraints; cooling systems manage waste heat. A substrate sustaining N joules of simulated activity must supply the corresponding computational throughput. The particulars only make the requirement legible: when one tries to imagine a substrate stripped of T, S, and Φ, one finds oneself imagining no substrate at all. The very features that would make it a hosting substrate are the ones being stripped.

So the substrate is not ontologically lighter than the simulated world but an additional extended manifold stacked behind it, running on its own structural cycle. The hypothesis multiplies T-S-Φ instantiation rather than reducing it, and relocates the structural cost rather than eliminating it. The appeal of simulation (that we get to keep the phenomenology without paying the structural cost) terminates where it began, with another T-S-Φ-instantiating system doing the hosting.

The same requirement bites on the other classic hypotheses. If our reality is a dream in the mind of a Cartesian demon, the demon's cognitive architecture must undergo causally structured transitions to produce the dream's content (T), differentiate the elements of its cognitive states to produce the dream's variety (S), and possess a medium of cognitive persistence connecting one dream-state to the next (Φ). And if we are Boltzmann brains, fleeting fluctuations in an entropic void, even the fluctuation must be an event in Physicality (Φ), occurring in temporal succession (T), at a position differentiated from its surroundings (S).

The concrete pattern generalizes to any **causal hosting** hierarchy. If reality₁ is produced or processed by reality₂, then reality₂ must instantiate temporal succession, differentiated vehicle-elements, and a persistent causal realizer. If reality₂ is causally hosted by reality₃, the same typed requirement applies. This is stronger than the general grounding claim because causal hosting supplies the type-upgrades directly. A purely atemporal grounding relation remains governed by the thinner role-level conclusion above.

*The Triconditional Cross-Entailment.* This line (developed at [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6)) works inside the domain of full change-realizers. It does not claim that every abstract order, geometry, or bearer carries all three Conditions; it claims that where one Condition is fully instantiated as part of genuine change, the other two are co-instantiated.

T, S, and Φ are analytically interdependent: the full instantiation of any one structurally requires the others. The claim is used here in advance of its derivation and stands or falls with it. Temporal succession without a persistence medium (Φ) is not a transition through which anything survives or occurs but a list of unrelated snapshots; temporal succession without a relational structure (S) is a bare ordering with no differentiated positions, and so not an order of anything at all. If these entailments hold, then the Cartesian certainty of T alone analytically carries S and Φ with it; the extension from the Cartesian premise to the full structure requires no further empirical premise. The *Cogito*, which establishes T with unconditional force, already contains S and Φ analytically. It survives even if one brackets hosts, substrates, and all appeal to output-constraints. The argument asks only whether Temporality can be fully instantiated without the other two, and if not, the extension is already complete.

*The Encoding Dilemma.* If the first works by the structure of grounding and the second by the internal entailment of the Conditions, the third works by turning the deflationist's own escape against it, and needs neither the grounding-priority premise of the first nor the cross-entailment of the second. It is stated and proved as the Constitutive Instantiation result at [§2.6.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-7), and it carries no premise about what production transmits. Its force is a dilemma. A candidate ground of an actually structured experience either instantiates the experienced Conditions outright or merely *encodes* them, and an encoding that grounds a live experience is itself a tokened structure, so either horn delivers a structured ground. This is why the simulation, demon, and Boltzmann-brain cases above bite as hard as they do: each is the encoding horn made concrete, a substrate that must *process* states (T), *differentiate* elements (S), and *sustain* a medium (Φ) to encode the experience it grounds.

::: {.corollary}
**Constitutive Instantiation** · **R8** · *Result of T3*

Where one of the Conditions (Temporality, Spatiality, or Physicality, or a determinate of one) is actually present in an experiencing, instantiated and not merely represented in content, all three are co-instantiated in that experiencing; and because the experiencing is a state its ground is in rather than a content the ground merely represents, the ground itself instantiates all three. And a ground reaches the same conclusion on either horn of a dilemma: if it instantiates the experienced Condition outright, directly; if it merely encodes it, then by tokening that encoding (borne in a medium, across distinct elements, processed across steps) it instantiates the Conditions all the same. A system can encode a Condition in the abstract without instantiating it, but it cannot ground a live experience in which that Condition is actually present without instantiating Temporality, Spatiality, and Physicality. ([§2.6.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-7))


:::

A two-dimensional game engine can *encode* a three-dimensional world by projection, but the encoding itself runs on a substrate with the spatial structure required to compute and store it; the engine's hardware is three-dimensional even when its rendered output is displayed on a two-dimensional surface. Constitutive Instantiation does not deny that lower-dimensional encodings of higher-dimensional structures exist; it requires that whatever *instantiates* the higher-dimensional structure as such (not as encoded representation but as the feature actually present in experience) must itself instantiate the Conditions that make that feature coherent. A system that lacks the structural Conditions can encode them in a representation but cannot host an experience in which those Conditions are actually present rather than merely represented. The result needs no premise about what causation transmits: on either horn of the dilemma, the actual presence of a structured Condition in the experience a ground sustains is instantiated in that ground; and the encoding/instantiation distinction marks where the result bites and where it does not.

*Applied to the ground of experience.* Our experience exhibits causally structured succession, relational extension, and causal persistence. Whatever constitutes the ground of this experience (physical medium, divine mind, Kantian transcendental subject, simulation substrate) must itself instantiate these three structural features for them to be actually present in the experience it hosts. The result thereby closes the extension from the Cartesian certainty of experience to the structural character of its ground: a Condition actually present in an experiencing co-instantiates all three within that experiencing by the cross-entailment, and because the experiencing is a state its ground is in rather than a content the ground merely represents (the realizer reading of [§2.6.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-1)), those Conditions are the ground's own.

*The emergence objection.* Liquidity emerges from molecules that are not liquid; life emerges from chemistry that is not alive. The pattern is real, and its credentials are honest. The objection (that novel structural properties can arise from substrates that do not individually possess them) does not defeat the result, because the result is not a claim about what individual components can produce but about what the system as a whole must instantiate once the feature is actually present. Whether the emergence is weak (macro-properties deducible from micro-dynamics) or strong (genuinely novel causal powers), the system in which those powers are actually instantiated must itself instantiate temporal succession, spatial distinctness, and a causal medium; emergence may relocate where a structural feature is first instantiated, but it cannot convert actual instantiation into mere encoding. Emergence moves the argument; it does not escape it.

*Weight of the three.* Level-invariance is the general line, but its conclusion is role-level. The Cross-Entailment is stronger in content and narrower in domain: it applies to full change-realizers. The Encoding Dilemma is narrower still, applying to tokened grounds of actual, ongoing experience. Its temporal step does not cover a frozen, never-read encoding. The lines therefore reinforce one another by covering different escape strategies, not by independently proving one unrestricted conclusion.

*What converges.* Any ground of actual structured experience must at minimum realize directed priority, differentiation, and bearing. Concrete causal or computational grounds instantiate richer temporal, spatial, and persistent types. Full change-realizers fall under the restricted Cross-Entailment, while tokened encodings fall under the Encoding Dilemma. A critic may resist one line without thereby defeating the others, but the conclusion carried forward must remain at the resolution and within the domain of the line that earned it.

### 2.2.3 Witness's Reach {#sec-2-2-3}

Four clarifications fix what the witness establishes, and what it does not. The third carries the objection that presses hardest on the witness.

*First.* The witness is positive: change is actual, and what is actual is possible, Cartesian-certain by the performative catch of [§2.2.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-2-1). What follows from it alone is therefore ◇C, and no necessity whatever. The necessity of the Conditions enters only once that possibility is lifted to □◇C by the Necessary Possibility Theorem ([§2.1.10](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-10)) and carried through the Structural Requirement ([§2.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-4)), and what is necessary at that point is the Conditions, not any specific configuration. That change is actual does not entail that any particular change must occur in any particular way, or that any specific medium takes any specific form. The necessity of the structure is the necessity of the Conditions; the contingency of specific configurations within those roles is preserved. The Modal Identity ([§2.6.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-6)) and the type/token distinction ([§6.6](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-6)) elaborate this distinction.

*Second.* The witness does not establish that the ground of experience is mind-independent physical reality. The level-invariance argument ([§2.2.2](the-argument.html#sec-2-2-2)) establishes that whatever the ground is (physical or transcendental) it instantiates T, S, and Φ. The argument's conclusion therefore does not depend on resolving the realism/idealism dispute.
